source: Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler & Sweller (2003) The expertise reversal effect, Educational Psychologist 38(1) 23-31
finding: Founding review. Guidance that helps low-knowledge learners (integrated text in diagrams, extra explanation, auditory text, worked examples) becomes redundant for experienced learners and then hurts or is neutral. Explained by cognitive load: redundant guidance must be reconciled with the expert's own schemas, so it adds extraneous load.
numbers: Review of earlier experiments. Worked-example study used mechanical-trade apprentices: novices who studied examples did better on the test and reported lower load than those who solved problems; with more experience the advantage vanished and problem solving was superior. No sample sizes in the summary I read.
quote: With more experience in the domain, the superiority of worked examples disappeared.
limits: I read only a Substack summary of the 2003 paper, not the paper (publisher PDF returned an HTML stub or 403). Numbers must be checked against the original.
agent_relevance: Core claim for S0: the right amount of help depends on the learner's current knowledge, and too much help is a cost, not a neutral extra.

source: Kalyuga (2007) Expertise reversal effect and its implications for learner-tailored instruction, Educ Psychol Rev 19, 509-539
finding: Review of expertise reversal research since the mid-1990s. Links the effect to aptitude-treatment interaction (ATI) studies from the mid-1960s (Cronbach and Snow 1977). Draws implications for adaptive learning systems that tailor support to measured knowledge.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Springer full text is behind a login redirect.
agent_relevance: ATI history says cross-over ideas are old and have failed to replicate before; test on our own logs rather than assume.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Expertise reversal effect: summary of studies it cites
finding: Lists studies that show the cross-over. Renkl and Atkinson (2003): worked examples beat problem solving for low-knowledge learners, and open problem solving beats examples as knowledge grows. Cooper et al. (2001): imagining procedures helps higher-knowledge learners, studying helps low-knowledge. Kalyuga et al. (1998): integrating split sources helps low-knowledge, removing the redundant source helps higher-knowledge. Spanjers et al. (2011): segmented animation helped low-knowledge learners; performance did not differ for high-knowledge, but effort and efficiency did.
numbers: The page gives no sample sizes or effect sizes for any of these.
limits: Secondary source. The page itself has no numbers. Spanjers shows the cost for experts can appear in effort and efficiency, not only in score.
agent_relevance: Measure cost as well as accuracy: help can leave the pass rate flat while it wastes tokens. A fading test should log tokens per solved item, not only pass rate.

source: Wikipedia reference list for the effect (Kalyuga 1998, 2000, 2001, 2004; Schnotz 2010; Salden 2008)
finding: Reference list names the main sources to follow backward: Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller (1998) Levels of expertise and instructional design, Human Factors 40:1-17; Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller (2000) J Educ Psych 92:126-136; Kalyuga et al. (2001) when problem solving beats worked examples; Schnotz (2010) Reanalyzing the expertise reversal effect, Instr Sci 38:315-323; Kalyuga, Rikers and Paas (2012) Educ Psychol Rev 24:313-337.
numbers: Citations only.
limits: Titles and venues only. These original papers were not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Backward chain for later agents: the 1998 electrical-circuit and 2001 worked-example experiments hold the numbers still needed.

source: Leppink & van den Heuvel (2015) The evolution of cognitive load theory and its application to medical education, Perspect Med Educ
finding: Textbook-style statement of the effect inside CLT. Support that cuts extraneous load for novices (worked examples, completion tasks, non-specific goals, dual-mode presentation, split-attention avoidance) may be redundant for proficient learners and then adds extraneous load. Advice: monitor proficiency and fade support.
numbers: No effect sizes or numbers for the effect. Intrinsic load is tied to the number of elements processed at once; expertise lowers it because schemas chunk elements.
quote: instructional support in a learning task that is beneficial for novice learners loses its effectiveness or even becomes detrimental
limits: Secondary review. Notes that earlier load-measurement studies did not address the effect.
agent_relevance: Supports a simple rule for S0: more expertise means fewer elements to hold, so a scaffold that carried those elements becomes overhead.

source: Chen, Kalyuga & Sweller (2017) The expertise reversal effect is a variant of the more general element interactivity effect, Educ Psychol Rev 29
finding: Argues the expertise reversal effect is a special case of the element interactivity effect. Both depend on how many interacting elements the learner must hold at once. Material complexity or the learner's expertise can change that number.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Springer full text not accessible. The 2016 date in our SUBFIELDS row is the online-first year; print year is 2017.
agent_relevance: Gives a computable handle: help is worth giving only when the item has many interacting steps relative to what the model already chunks.

source: Blayney, Kalyuga & Sweller (2016) The impact of complexity on the expertise reversal effect: accounting students, Educational Psychology
finding: Isolating elements helped novices. Presenting interacting elements together suited more knowledgeable learners, but only for high element-interactivity material.
numbers: N = 104 students.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Shows the reversal depends on task complexity, a boundary condition.
agent_relevance: A hard item may still need help for a strong class. Gate on item complexity as well as class pass rate.

source: Chen, Retnowati & Kalyuga (2020) Element interactivity as a factor influencing worked example-problem solving and problem solving-worked example sequences, Br J Educ Psychol
finding: Worked-example-first beat problem-first for high element-interactivity material, especially for novices. At low element interactivity the sequences did not differ for more knowledgeable learners.
numbers: Experiment 1: 52 Year-5 students in Indonesia. Experiment 2: 96 Year-8 students. 2x2 design.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Children in mathematics tasks only.
agent_relevance: Same lesson: the help-or-not choice is item by item, not only class by class.

source: Chen, Retnowati & Kalyuga (2019) Effects of worked examples on step performance in solving complex problems, Educational Psychology
finding: Novices gained from worked examples mostly at the hardest step (Step 1), little or none at the easiest step (Step 3). More knowledgeable participants showed no worked-example effect overall or at any step.
numbers: Two experiments. Sample sizes not in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Step-level result: help pays where element interactivity is highest.
agent_relevance: Fade help step by step, not per whole problem: keep it on the hard step, drop it from the easy ones.

source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck & Boshuizen (2013) Worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: legal cases, Contemp Educ Psychol
finding: Failure to find the reversal. Worked examples beat problem solving for both novice and advanced law students.
numbers: Four support conditions; two expertise groups. Sample sizes not in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Less structured task. Advanced students were not true experts, so the group may have been too close to novices.
agent_relevance: In open, ill-structured tasks the cross-over may not appear. Do not fade help on open-mode items on the strength of well-structured studies.

source: Darabi & Nelson (2004) Training and transfer of complex cognitive skills: worked examples vs conventional problem solving (ED485099)
finding: Chemical engineering seniors troubleshooting a plant simulation: no group difference between process-oriented worked examples, product-oriented worked examples and conventional problem solving. The authors read this as consistent with expertise reversal.
numbers: 36 senior students, 3 groups, 4 training malfunctions, 8 near-transfer problems and 1 far-transfer task. No significant differences.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). A null result read as support for the theory after the fact; weak evidence for the cross-over itself.
agent_relevance: A null effect for experts is the weak form (help is useless). The strong form (help hurts) needs a negative effect.

source: Binmahfooz (2019) Graphics visualizations and expertise reversal on engineering students (ED637968)
finding: Dissertation found no expertise reversal. Graphic type and expertise each had significant effects on achievement and motivation, but no significant interaction.
numbers: Sequential vs simultaneous graphic videos, novice vs expert engineering students. Sample size not in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Dissertation, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Unpublished failures exist; treat the effect as likely but not universal.

source: Rey & Fischer (2013) The expertise reversal effect concerning instructional explanations, Instructional Science
finding: Effect found for transfer but not for retention. Expertise was induced by adding expository examples and illustrations.
numbers: 2x2 between-subjects, N = 93 students, statistics in a computer environment.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Partial replication: outcome measure matters.
agent_relevance: Check both near and far tests when measuring fading; the cross-over may show on only one.

source: Rey & Buchwald (2011) The expertise reversal effect: cognitive load and motivational explanations, J Exp Psychol Appl
finding: Extra explanatory text helped novices on retention and transfer and reversed for experts. Results favoured a cognitive-load account over a motivational (boredom) account.
numbers: N = 104 students; about 30 minutes learning gradient descent; 2x2 design.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Competing explanation (motivation) was tested and not supported.
agent_relevance: A model has no boredom, so load is the only mechanism that could carry over to an LLM.

source: Oksa, Kalyuga & Chandler (2010) Expertise reversal in explanatory notes for Shakespearean text, Instructional Science
finding: Notes lowered load and raised comprehension for novices (Experiments 1 and 3, a different play in Exp 3). The benefit reversed for Shakespeare experts (Experiment 2).
numbers: Three experiments. Sample sizes not in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Replicated across two plays for novices, one group of experts.
agent_relevance: A clean cross-over in text understanding: help for the weak group, harm for the strong group.

source: Reisslein, Atkinson, Seeling & Reisslein (2006) Encountering the expertise reversal effect with a computer-based environment on electrical circuit analysis, Learn Instr
finding: Three example-based procedures (example-problem, problem-example, fading) for series and parallel circuits at two prior-knowledge levels. Low-knowledge learners did best with example-problem pairs; high-knowledge learners did best with problem-example pairs.
numbers: Two prior-knowledge levels, three procedures. Sample sizes not in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). The abstract does not say fading won for either group.
agent_relevance: In circuits, ordering (example first or problem first) mattered, and fading was not shown as a universal fix.

source: Salden, Aleven, Schwonke & Renkl (2010) The expertise reversal effect and worked examples in tutored problem solving, Instr Sci 38, 289-307
finding: A Cognitive Tutor with adaptive fading of worked steps (tied to each student's understanding) beat fixed fading in both a lab and a classroom experiment. Fixed fading beat plain problem solving.
numbers: One lab experiment and one classroom experiment; the abstract has no numerals.
limits: I read only the abstract page; exact N and scores not seen. Ordering is adaptive > fixed fading > problem solving only.
agent_relevance: Direct support for adaptive fading by measured knowledge, which is what S0 would do by class pass rate.

source: Kissane, Kalyuga, Chandler & Sweller (2008) Consequences of fading instructional guidance on delayed performance: financial services training, Educational Psychology
finding: Gradual fading of worked examples beat example-problem pairs and beat pure problem solving, on delayed and transfer posttests.
numbers: Three conditions in a classroom of financial-services employees; measures immediate and delayed; the abstract says the advantages were statistically significant.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Adult workplace sample; N not given in abstract.
agent_relevance: Fading wins on delayed tests, so judge fading on later items, not just the next item.

source: Renkl, Atkinson & Grosse (2004) How fading worked solution steps works: a cognitive load perspective, Instr Sci 32
finding: Learners learned most about the principles that were faded. Position of the faded step did not matter. Fading went with fewer unproductive learning events (think-aloud), not more self-explanation.
numbers: Two experiments, one with think-aloud protocols. Sample sizes not in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Mechanism evidence: fading works by removing unproductive events.
agent_relevance: Fade the parts we want the model to do itself; the faded content is what it learns to do.

source: Nuckles, Hubner, Dumer & Renkl (2010) Expertise reversal effects in writing-to-learn, Instr Sci
finding: In two longitudinal journal-writing studies, prompts helped early in a term but the advantage faded as students became skilled. Gradual, adaptive fading of prompts (Experiment 2) did better than permanent prompts.
numbers: Two longitudinal studies. Sample sizes not in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Shows reversal over time within the same learners, not only between groups.
agent_relevance: A class that improves over a run should see help withdrawn during that run, not only at the start.

source: Leppink, Broers, Imbos, van der Vleuten & Berger (2012) Self-explanation in statistics: an expertise reversal effect, Higher Education
finding: Low prior-knowledge students learned most from worked examples; high prior-knowledge students benefited most from formulating arguments (self-explanation).
numbers: Four instructional methods compared for low and high prior knowledge.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). The better method for experts was an active task, not just no help.
agent_relevance: For strong classes replace help with a demand to produce an argument, not with nothing.

source: Pawley, Ayres, Cooper & Sweller (2005) Translating words into equations (EJ691099)
finding: Checking instruction plus worked examples first disadvantaged students. After more practice, low-knowledge students gained from checking while higher-knowledge students stayed disadvantaged.
numbers: Two experiments with Grade 8 and 9 students.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Sample sizes not in abstract.
agent_relevance: Step checking (our S4 style) could be redundant for strong classes; check this in our logs.

source: Johnson-Glenberg (2010) Embedded formative e-assessment: who benefits, who falters
finding: Embedded quizzes helped low-experience tutors learn more than expert tutors, a classic reversal. The quiz-with-warning condition added no main effect.
numbers: 178 participants randomly assigned to control, quiz, or quiz-with-warning.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Testing as support, not only explanation.
agent_relevance: Extra verification steps may help weak solvers and slow strong ones.

source: Jiang, Kalyuga & Sweller (2018) Improving foreign language listening by reading rather than listening: an expertise reversal effect, Educ Psychol Rev
finding: Four experiments: read-only helped more expert learners (Exp 1 and 2); read-and-listen helped novices (Exp 3 and 4). Native Chinese speakers learning English (Exp 1-3) or French (Exp 4).
numbers: Four experiments; sample sizes not in the abstract.
limits: ERIC API record (abstract only, paraphrased by fetch tool; full paper not opened). Replicated across two target languages.
agent_relevance: Domain breadth: language as well as mechanics, circuits and programming.

source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters & Brod (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity: a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect, Learning and Instruction 98, 102142
finding: First meta-analysis of the effect (title and CC BY licence confirmed from Crossref). Results not read: the publisher page returned 403, the Elsevier text API 400, and Crossref has no abstract.
numbers: Crossref: 69 references. Pooled effect size and moderators NOT obtained.
limits: Only metadata seen. This is the single most important paper still to open; it is CC BY.
agent_relevance: Would give the pooled size and moderators (task type, expertise measure) needed to set our fading threshold.

source: He-Yueya, Goodman & Brunskill (2024) Evaluating and optimizing educational content with large language model judgments, arXiv 2403.02795
finding: Used GPT-3.5 as a simulated educational expert predicting post-test scores for 120 student personas (skill levels 1 to 5). The LM reproduced the cross-over: low-expertise personas scored higher after worked examples than after practice, with no significant difference for high-expertise personas. The pattern appeared again in a second run built for the variability effect.
numbers: n = 120 personas; worked-example vs practice; 8 word problems (worked solutions for problems 1, 3, 5, 7); gpt-3.5-turbo-16k, temperature 0; algebra word problems. The paper gives plots with standard-error bars, no numeric table I could read.
quote: LM-based simulated expert evaluations can replicate the Expertise Reversal Effect
limits: The LM judges predicted scores; nothing was learned by a real learner. The authors note it may have seen the original studies, and that LMs were poor simulators of actual student learning. The result is the weak form: no gain for experts, not a harm.
agent_relevance: LLMs carry the folk theory of the effect. Do not rely on a model to decide when to fade; use measured pass rates (G5: code selects).

source: He-Yueya et al. (2024) Instruction Optimization, section 4 (same paper)
finding: An optimizer LM (GPT-4) wrote new worksheets for a persona and an evaluator LM (gpt-3.5) predicted the post-test score. Scores climbed over optimisation steps until they converged. The persona in the example prompt had skill level 1 out of 5.
numbers: Optimizer gpt-4, evaluator gpt-3.5-turbo-16k; starting worksheet predicted score 20 for a level-1 persona; about 18 optimisation steps plotted.
limits: Optimised against the same evaluator LM, so gains may exploit the judge, not the learner. No human check.
agent_relevance: Shows the loop form: persona-conditioned help generation. It also shows the risk named in G5: models favour their own text.

source: Wu et al. (2026) SLATE: are AI-generated slides educationally effective? arXiv 2609.06212
finding: Student-model ablation: slides raised learning gain for 3 of 4 student models, but the smallest model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) had a negative slide effect (about 1.4 points). The authors call this consistent with expertise reversal, but their explanation is overload from too little capacity, which is a different cause from the usual one.
numbers: Slide effects across the four student models (by size): 1.4 (negative), 4.3, 4.0, 5.0 percent; signs for the positives inferred from the text. Benchmark pretest baseline 23.78%. 90 instructional units, 1,133 items. Judges: Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini-3.1-Pro, GPT-5.4.
quote: instructional scaffolding that benefits intermediate learners can impose extraneous cognitive load on learners whose processing capacity is insufficient
limits: Mislabel risk: a weak learner hurt by help is a capacity limit, not expertise reversal. Minus signs were lost in PDF text extraction. Not a controlled test of the effect.
agent_relevance: A low-capacity model can be hurt by long scaffolds; shorten them for weak models, not only for strong ones.

source: Wu et al. (2026) SLATE appendix G: failure cases at high baseline
finding: Two decks produced large drops where the student model already scored high. Jahai smell-verb deck (Gemini-3.1-Pro): pretest 72%, a rigid six-way schema overwrote flexible prior knowledge, with a large posttest drop (printed as about 50 points). Dutch spelling deck (GPT-5.4): pretest 70%, posttest 40%, gain -30, near transfer 100%, far transfer 50%. The authors call both expertise reversal.
numbers: Jahai: pretest 72%, gain printed as about -50. Dutch: 70% to 40%, near 100%, far 50%. Authors hypothesise format-induced response shift (transfer-appropriate processing).
quote: a pattern consistent with the expertise reversal effect, in which instructional scaffolding designed for novices actively harms learners with relevant prior knowledge
limits: Single decks, no replicates; causes are the authors' hypotheses. The Dutch deck taught the rules (near transfer 100%) yet scores fell, so a format shift is an equally good account.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can change the answer format and lose points the model already had. At high baseline, check output format before blaming content.

source: Hou et al. (2026) Adaptive scaffolding needs contingency: an AI tutor that escalates and fades, arXiv 2609.22993 (CoMeT)
finding: A contingent LLM tutor raises support after failure and fades on take-up. In a within-subject test it matched the question-only tutor's metacognitive demand, delivered artifacts about twice as often, and frustrated learners less than the question-only tutor. Load and delegation did not change. Fading held when the learner's turn was aimed at the decision under support.
numbers: 131 adult learners, 3 Python tasks, 393 sessions, 3 tutors. 551 fading episodes, 515 coded; only 282 followed a direct answer. Later concessions: 30.3% after full demonstration, 25.9% after pasted artifact, 20.4% after bare assertion, 33.7% after build request; 40.3% (72 open decisions) when not aimed at the decision vs 28.8% (1,084) when aimed, difference 11.5 points, 95% CI [2.1, 22.4]. Full answer given away: 59.5% Tutor A, 16.0% Tutor B, 6.1% Tutor C (about 1 in 16).
limits: Does not test expertise reversal directly and has no novice-expert split. Programming learners only. In the extracted table the Tutor B and C rows are printed out of order, so which of 16.0 and 6.1 belongs to B is taken from the text (C is the lower).
agent_relevance: Best LLM evidence on fading in practice: success need not be a correct answer; fade when the attempt targets the right sub-decision. Fading on an off-target turn was wrong 40% of the time.

source: EPFL study (2026) Reflective dialogue or prompt refinement? Socratic vs prompt-refinement GPT-5 tutors, arXiv 2607.03303
finding: Graduate robotics course. Socratic-guidance students started with lower pretests but gained more pre-to-post in session 3. The paper does not discuss expertise reversal.
numbers: 172 enrolled, 66 attended S3, 52 used the project chatbot. S3 pretest SG lower (beta = -0.52, p = .02); interaction beta = 0.72, p = .01. No condition effect on prompting in S3 (chi2 = 1.12, p = .77). SG lower on S1 task (beta = -0.8, p = .001).
limits: I read an alphaxiv summary, not the paper. Groups differed on pretest, so gain comparisons are fragile. No expertise split analysed.
agent_relevance: Less help (Socratic) did not hurt a graduate sample, but this is not evidence about experts versus novices.

source: Search note (2023) Other LLM-era appeals to the effect: formative-feedback prompts, arXiv 2311.13984
finding: An LLM formative-feedback paper (2311.13984) designs prompts so feedback fires only when a student answer is incomplete or wrong, citing load from repeating known content. No test of the effect.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Known only from a search snippet; not opened. The search budget ran out, so further 2020-2026 LLM tests were not found.
agent_relevance: Design precedent for gating help on a failure signal, which matches G1.
